outcome: The question remains unresolved; the only development since 26 January 2024 is a continued computational extension of the sequence (Ben Chaffin, reaching over 10^612 terms as of a page dated 7 February 2026) confirming 852655 is still the smallest number not yet found in the sequence. This narrows nothing about the existence question itself (§3.1) and no proof, disproof, or new analytic bound was found.
summary: This is an existence/infinitude-shaped question ('does every nonnegative integer appear?'), which per §3.1 is advanced only by an actual answer, not by extending a computational search. I found no proof, disproof, partial resolution, or new analytic bound published since 26 January 2024. What did happen in the window is a further extension of Ben Chaffin's long-running brute-force computation of the sequence: his project page (dated 7 February 2026) reports over 10^612 terms computed on custom hardware (Intel Skylake system, 256GB RAM, 30TB disk, ~14 months of runtime) with 852655 still the smallest integer absent from the sequence — the same status that has held since it was first identified missing around 2018 (and known missing since at least 2001, when all numbers below it had appeared). OEIS A005132 and Wikipedia's own article corroborate this figure and status, and explicitly state the conjecture (originally made by Neil Sloane in 1991, and which Sloane himself walked back in 2017, saying 'today I'm not so sure that every number appears') remains open with no proof either way. I searched specifically for any AI/LLM involvement in this computation or in any recent theoretical work on the conjecture and found none — the extension is a straightforward (if computationally heavy) brute-force enumeration using classical algorithmic speedups (exploiting 'ping-pong' range patterns), not a mathematical or AI-driven advance on the open question. No arXiv paper, blog post, or announcement in the window claims progress on the actual existence question. Per §3.1, a computational search extended further, without an answer, does not count as a change to this bullet.
competing_reading: One could argue the repeated confirmation that 852655 remains missing after an enormous further extension of the search (10^230 in 2018 to 10^612 in 2026) is itself informative evidence shifting expert opinion toward 852655 never appearing (i.e., toward the conjecture being false), and thus worth recording as 'progress' in an informal sense. But per the rubric's explicit rule in §3.1 ('a search verified to a larger limit... narrows where an answer could hide, not whether it exists'), this does not qualify as a status change, so I classified it as open/no_change_found rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a proof that every nonnegative integer must eventually appear (settling the conjecture affirmatively), or (b) a proof — or a computational discovery — that some specific number (e.g. 852655) can never appear, which would refute it. Short of that, only further computation narrowing the search continues, which does not change the classification.
